newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen president meets kin of Russian hostages.
newsitem.headline: Chechen president meets kin of Russian hostages.

text.p: The president of Chechnya Aslan Maskhadov met relatives of Russians kidnapped in the breakaway region at an encounter hosted by the secretary of the Kremlin Security Council on Tuesday, a council spokesman said.
Maskhadov, who was expected to leave Moscow shortly afterwards, pledged to find missing journalists and to make the work of law enforcement in Chechnya more efficient.
On Monday, he signed a peace accord in the Kremlin with Russian President Boris Yeltsin.

Chechen bandits have seized a number of Russian and foreign journalists, escalating tension in the region prior to the long-awaited peace treaty. The latest incident happened on Saturday when a Russian television crew was kidnapped.
The Chechen leadership blamed the "parties of war" wanting to thwart the peace process for the kidnappings and promised to bring those responsible to justice.
Moscow and Chechnya on Monday both promised to end 400 years of intermittent conflict. The deal aims to turn last year's ceasefire into a lasting peace.

The truce had halted a 21-month war in the predominantly Moslem region in which tens of thousands of people died. It included the withdrawal of Russian troops and the deferral of any decision on Chechen sovereignty until 2001.
Russian newspapers on Tuesday noted that the latest peace treaty left the question of Chechnya's sovereignty unclear.

"The text of the treaty is full of compromises and multi-meaning sentences; it can be interpreted in very many ways by different forces in Moscow and Grozny," said the liberal daily Nezavisimaya Gazeta.

Maskhadov has insisted on full independence from Russia. The treaty said relations between the region and Moscow would be in accordance with "norms of international law" but the Kremlin insisted there was still no question of Chechnya seceding.

Nezavisimaya said the very fact of a peace treaty between Moscow and Grozny was a great concession from the Kremlin, which had previously viewed treaties with entities within the Russian Federation as unacceptable.
But Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky reiterated on Tuesday that the treaty did not mean that Chechnya would become a subject under international law.
Yeltsin set up a special federal commission on Tuesday to deal with political and other issues in Chechnya and to work out draft agreements between Moscow and Grozny.
In Chechnya, locals hailed the peace treaty, calling the signing day a great day for the Chechen people.

"The document means peace, reconstruction of Grozny and all Chechnya," Rustam Goigov, 75, told Reuters in Grozny. "There are no totally independent republics -- all must have mutual links. We have our government and that makes us independent enough."
Tumisha Dadayeva, 60 , the mother of a guerilla fighter missed in action said with tears: "The signing gave me hope to find my missing son. Peace is a great thing for us Chechens."
But Nezavisimaya added a note of pessimism:
"Russian artillery and aviation have been demolishing Chechen towns for two years, but now a new approach has prevailed -- peace at any cost. Will it last long?"
